parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: absence of driving and damping forces
hints: Hint 1: Think about how the system would move if you pull it aside once and then let go completely, with nothing pushing it and nothing rubbing against it.
parts.proper_answer: The natural frequency is the frequency of free oscillation of a system with no driving force and no (resultant) resistive damping force.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture a free system**
Imagine pulling the mass on the spring down a little and then just releasing it. You are not keeping your hand on it to push it repeatedly, and imagine there is no air resistance or friction stealing energy. That back-and-forth motion left to itself is called a free oscillation.

Step 2: **Define the natural frequency**
Every such system has its own preferred rate of vibrating, fixed by things like mass $m$ and spring constant $k$. That single frequency of free vibration, with no external driving force and no damping, is the natural frequency $f_0$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the shape of Fig. 4.2 - the amplitude $x_0$ is small everywhere except for one sharp maximum at a particular driving frequency $f$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the resonance curve**
The oscillator at the top is forcing the block to vibrate at frequency $f$. At most values of $f$ the block barely moves, but at one special frequency the amplitude $x_0$ shoots up to a large peak. That large response when driving frequency equals natural frequency is resonance.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall what a resonance peak would look like with zero damping - the amplitude at resonance would grow without limit.
Hint 2: Now compare that idea with Fig. 4.2 where the peak is tall and sharp but still has a finite height - what does that tell you about energy loss?
parts.proper_answer: Yes, the oscillations are lightly damped. Damping must be present because the resonant amplitude is finite, but the damping is light because the peak is tall and sharp.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why damping must be present**
With no energy loss at all, feeding energy in at resonance on every cycle would make the amplitude $x_0$ grow and grow with no limit. Here in Fig. 4.2 the peak reaches a maximum finite value, so some energy must be being removed each cycle. That means damping forces such as air resistance are acting.

Step 2: **Why the damping is light**
Heavy damping would flatten the curve and give only a low, broad hump. This curve shows a high, narrow, sharp peak, which is the classic signature of light damping. So the block is undergoing lightly damped forced oscillations.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Think of a situation where you deliberately want a tiny push at the right frequency to build up into a big vibration or signal.
parts.proper_answer: Tuning a radio to a particular station, or a musical instrument sounding box, or microwave oven heating, or magnetic resonance imaging.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use resonance to pick out one frequency**
Resonance is very useful when you want maximum energy transfer from a weak driver. A good example is tuning an analogue radio: the circuit is adjusted so its natural frequency equals the frequency of the wanted radio wave, so it resonates and responds strongly to that station while ignoring others.
